proposals.before: Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital in early Yongchu (424–424) and given a lecture hall to live in.
proposals.after: Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital during Yongchu (420–422) and given a lecture hall to live in.
proposals.reason: 周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, not Zhou Xuanshi, and the Liu Song Yongchu era ran from 420 to 422.

proposals.before: Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; in the early Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.
proposals.after: Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; during the Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.
proposals.reason: 周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, and 永初中 means during the Yongchu era rather than necessarily its beginning.

proposals.before: The emperor set him to examine Xuanshi on the Three Meanings. Xuanshi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.
proposals.after: The emperor set him to examine Xuzhi on the Three Meanings. Xuzhi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.
proposals.reason: 續之 refers to Zhou Xuzhi; Xuanshi is a name error.

proposals.before: The emperor had him question Xuanshi on the Three Meanings; Xuanshi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.
proposals.after: The emperor had him question Xuzhi on the Three Meanings; Xuzhi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.
proposals.reason: 續之 refers to Zhou Xuzhi; Xuanshi is a name error.

proposals.before: After he had repeatedly bested Xuanshi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.
proposals.after: After he had repeatedly bested Xuzhi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.
proposals.reason: 續之 refers to Zhou Xuzhi; Xuanshi is a name error.

proposals.before: Having repeatedly defeated Xuanshi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.
proposals.after: Having repeatedly defeated Xuzhi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.
proposals.reason: 續之 refers to Zhou Xuzhi; Xuanshi is a name error.

proposals.before: Fu Liang, then Minister of Works, believed no one of the time could rival him in literary brilliance; Yanzhi, confident in his own gifts, refused to yield, and Liang came to detest him.
proposals.after: Fu Liang, then Director of the Imperial Secretariat, believed no one of the time could rival him in literary brilliance; Yanzhi, confident in his own gifts, refused to yield, and Liang came to detest him.
proposals.reason: 尚書令 is Director of the Imperial Secretariat, not Minister of Works.

proposals.before: At that time Minister of Works Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary meaning unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.
proposals.after: At that time Director of the Imperial Secretariat Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary expression unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.
proposals.reason: 尚書令 is Director of the Imperial Secretariat, not Minister of Works.

proposals.before: When Yanzhi went to his commandery, his route passed the Mi Pool; for Xiangzhou Inspector Zhang Shao he offered a sacrifice to Qu Yuan's text to convey his intent, saying:
proposals.after: When Yanzhi went to his commandery, his route passed the Mi Pool; for Xiangzhou Inspector Zhang Shao he composed a sacrificial text for Qu Yuan to convey his intent, saying:
proposals.reason: 祭屈原文 means to compose a sacrificial text for Qu Yuan, not to sacrifice to Qu Yuan's text.

proposals.before: Under Kings Ying and Qian strife arose; Kings Zhao and Huai lost their way.
proposals.after: Between the Ying and Qian ruling houses strife arose; Kings Zhao and Huai lost their way.
proposals.reason: 嬴 and 芊 designate ruling clan houses here, not kings named Ying and Qian.

proposals.before: Intrigue broke down Shang Yi; loyalty was mocked, and Jiao and Lan despised.
proposals.after: His plans thwarted Yi and Shang; his integrity scorned Jiao and Lan.
proposals.reason: 儀、尚 names two separate figures, Yi and Shang, in that order; the current translation fuses and reverses them.

proposals.before: Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. The Founder wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.
proposals.after: Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. Emperor Wen wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.
proposals.reason: 太祖 here is Emperor Wen Liu Yilong, not the Founder Gaozu Liu Yu.

proposals.before: At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. The Founder instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.
proposals.after: At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. Taizu instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.
proposals.reason: 太祖 is Taizu, Emperor Wen Liu Yilong, not Gaozu the Founder.

proposals.before: If you grasp that kindness and intent breed one another and that principle and feeling arise together, your household may hold men like Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be a Yan Hui or Min Sun.
proposals.after: If you grasp that kindness and intent breed one another and that principle and feeling arise together, your household may hold men like Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be a Zhong You or Min Sun.
proposals.reason: 由 abbreviates Zhong You (Zilu), not Yan Hui.

proposals.before: If one only knew that favor and intent give birth to each other and principle and feeling emerge from each other, one could make the family have Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be Yan Hui or Min Sun.
proposals.after: If one only knew that favor and intent give birth to each other and principle and feeling emerge from each other, one could make the family have Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be Zhong You or Min Sun.
proposals.reason: 由 abbreviates Zhong You (Zilu), not Yan Hui.

proposals.before: Once, drunk, he told the emperor: "In old times when the crown prince shared the carriage with others, Yuan Ang kept a stern countenance.
proposals.after: Once, drunk, he told the emperor: "In old times when Tongzi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang kept a stern countenance.
proposals.reason: 同子 is the Shiji taboo-avoidance name for the eunuch Zhao Tan, not a crown prince; the anecdote is Yuan Ang rebuking a eunuch riding with the emperor.

proposals.before: Drunk he told the Emperor: "In old times when Zisi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang showed stern color.
proposals.after: Drunk he told the Emperor: "In old times when Tongzi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang showed stern color.
proposals.reason: 同子 is not Zisi; it denotes the eunuch Tongzi (Zhao Tan) in the Yuan Ang carriage anecdote.

proposals.before: My son Jun is slight in talent and serves as magistrate of a nearby district; imperial favor has descended upon him, which only adds to my being watched—I beg to resign my offices and retire to medical care.
proposals.after: My son Fu is slight in talent and serves as magistrate of a nearby district; imperial favor has descended upon him, which only adds to my being watched—I beg to resign my offices and retire to medical care.
proposals.reason: 息㚟 names Yanzhi's third son 㚟 (Fu), not 竣 (Yan Jun); later units translate 㚟 as Fu and state he is the third son.

proposals.before: Son Jun is commonplace and slight, passing through near district as magistrate; favor and grace descended, truly adding my being overseen—I beg to resign my offices and follow to drug nurture.
proposals.after: Son Fu is commonplace and slight, passing through near district as magistrate; favor and grace descended, truly adding my being overseen—I beg to resign my offices and follow to drug nurture.
proposals.reason: Chinese 㚟 is the third son Fu, not Jun (竣).

proposals.before: He who can harden himself against his own parent will harden himself against others' parents; he who forgets his own filial duty expects to fulfill others'—as with Yi Yin who ate his son, or Duke Huan who freed the deer, the pattern is plain.
proposals.after: He who can harden himself against his own parent will harden himself against others' parents; he who forgets his own filial duty expects to fulfill others'—as with Yi Ya who cooked his son, or Duke Huan who freed the deer, the pattern is plain.
proposals.reason: 食子 in this topos refers to Yi Ya (易牙), who cooked his son for Duke Huan of Qi, not the Shang minister Yi Yin (伊尹).

proposals.before: One who can bear against his own parent will surely bear against others' parents; one who forgets his own filial piety expects to extend others' filial piety—Yi Yin who ate his son and Duke Huan who released the deer: this can clearly be known.
proposals.after: One who can bear against his own parent will surely bear against others' parents; one who forgets his own filial piety expects to extend others' filial piety—Yi Ya who ate his son and Duke Huan who released the deer: this can clearly be known.
proposals.reason: 食子 points to Yi Ya (易牙), not Yi Yin.

decisions.reason: 周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, and 永初中 places the summons in the Liu Song Yongchu era (420–422); ‘Xuanshi’ and the nonsensical (424–424) dating are translation errors.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 雁門人周續之……永初中，徵詣京師

decisions.reason: 周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, and 永初中 means during Yongchu, not necessarily its beginning; ‘Xuanshi’ and ‘early’ are unsupported.
續之 continues the previously named 周續之 (Zhou Xuzhi); ‘Xuanshi’ is a carry-over name error.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 上使問續之三義，續之雅仗辭辯

decisions.reason: 續之 is Zhou Xuzhi; replacing ‘Xuanshi’ restores the correct short name.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 問續之三義，續之雅仗辭辯

decisions.reason: 既連挫續之 refers to defeating Zhou Xuzhi; ‘Xuanshi’ is wrong.
挫續之 names Zhou Xuzhi; the proposed short form Xuzhi matches the Chinese.
尚書令 is Director of the Imperial Secretariat; Minister of Works renders 司空, which is not in the text.

decisions.after: At that time Director of the Imperial Secretariat Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary meaning unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.
decisions.reason: 尚書令 must be corrected from Minister of Works, but 文義之美 is literary meaning, not ‘expression’; keep the accurate original wording for that phrase.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 時尚書令傅亮自以文義之美

decisions.reason: 祭屈原文 is composing a sacrificial text for Qu Yuan, not sacrificing to Qu Yuan’s text.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 為湘州刺史張邵祭屈原文以致其意

decisions.reason: 嬴、芊 are clan houses paired with royal designations 昭、懷; ‘Kings Ying and Qian’ invents personal king-names the Chinese does not use.
儀、尚 are two figures in that order, parallel to 椒、蘭; ‘Shang Yi’ fuses and reverses the names, and the proposed agent reading matches 謀/貞.
In this Yuanjia-context passage 太祖 is Emperor Wen (Liu Yilong), not Gaozu the Founder (高祖).
Literal should render 太祖 as Taizu (Emperor Wen), not ‘the Founder’, which belongs to 高祖.
人皆由、損 pairs 由 (Zhong You / Zilu) with 損 (Min Sun); Yan Hui would be 回, which is not here.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 可使家有參、柴，人皆由、損

decisions.reason: 由 abbreviates Zhong You, not Yan Hui; the proposed literal matches 由、損.
同子參乘 is the Tongzi (Zhao Tan) carriage anecdote; ‘crown prince’ invents a figure the Chinese does not name, and the next sentence’s 刑餘 confirms a eunuch.
同子 is Tongzi, not Zisi; the proposed literal restores the correct name.
息㚟 names the son 㚟 (Fu), not 竣 (Jun); the character in the Chinese is 㚟.
㚟 is Fu; ‘Jun’ is a wrong identification of a different son’s name.
食子放鹿 paired with Duke Huan is the Yi Ya (易牙) cooked-son topos, not Shang minister Yi Yin; the replacement restores the correct allusion.
食子 in this couplet denotes Yi Ya, not Yi Yin; the literal name fix is required.

claimRetractions.reason: Accepted r0020 shows the 食子 figure is Yi Ya, not Yi Yin; the ‘statesman’ role was inferred only from that false Shang-minister identification and has no support in 食子放鹿.

claimRevisions.reason: Accepted r0020 restores the 食子 allusion to Yi Ya; the English name claim must read Yi Ya, and certainty drops to strongly-inferred because the Chinese does not write the name out.
With Yi Ya restored, the Shang-era attestation interval for Yi Yin is invalid; align the dates with Duke Huan of Qi’s reign, the setting of the cooked-son anecdote.
